title: Association Among Eating Speed, Dietary Diversity, and Fat‐Free Mass Index in Adults
html:
This study examined the associations among body composition indices, eating speed, and dietary diversity. Dietary diversity was positively associated with muscle mass in men and negatively associated with body fat mass index in women, while fast eating was significantly associated with fat-free mass index.


ABSTRACT

Objective

Dietary diversity and eating behaviour are recognised as factors influencing body composition; however, their association with fat-free mass index and body fat mass index remains unclear.

Methods

This cross-sectional study analysed the relationships among body composition indices (BMI, FFMI, BFMI), self-reported eating speed, and dietary diversity in 10 644 healthy adults aged 18–64 years (4419 women and 6225 men; mean age 41.9 years) who visited hospitals for health checkups.

Results

The dietary variety score showed a positive association with muscle mass in men and a significant negative association with body fat mass index in women (fat-free mass index: β = 0.03, 95% confidence interval: 0.01 to 0.05, p = 0.04; body fat mass index: β = −0.07, 95% confidence interval: −0.15 to −0.01, p < 0.01). Regarding eating speed, a consistent trend was observed in both sexes: the fast-eating group showed significantly higher body mass index, fat-free mass index, and body fat mass index values (p < 0.01), whereas the slow-eating group had lower values.

Conclusions

These associations were more pronounced in men than in women. Both dietary diversity and eating speed were associated with body composition indices, with notable sex-related differences. These findings suggest that dietary behaviour and diversity may influence body composition.
